title: Center for Refugee Studies Op-Ed Initiative Webinar Series
description: The CRS Op-Ed Initiative, open to faculty, students, and the CRS community, teaches participants how to convert research insights into accessible, public-facing op-eds. This four-course series covers how to develop, write, edit, and publish op-eds, and why opinion writing is an important vessel for spreading innovative ideas and sparking important discussions. Participants do not need any prior publication experience to join, and the course is free.The series is led by Assistant Director Meredith Perkins, who has six years of experience writing over 50 op-eds as a freelance journalist in student, local, and national publications. She won the 2024 and 2025 Region 4 Society of Professional Journalists Best College Opinion Writing award and the 2023 Ohio News Media Association Best Collegiate Column Writing award. A current Master of Public Affairs-Master of International Affairs student, her past newsroom experience inspires her to make complex academic conversations accessible for public audiences.Session 1: Before You Writewill introduce the history and purpose of op-eds and the range of places where opinion writing appears, including local and national newspapers, industry publications, departmental blogs, and platforms such as Substack. We will review genre conventions of op-eds, why op-eds are useful, and what information writers should know (e.g. workplace media policies) before considering publication.Session 2: Drafting Your First Op-Edwill focus on identifying a strong and timely argument. Participants will examine who is already writing about their topic, the dominant conversation surrounding it, and recent news or research that might create an opportunity for commentary. A central exercise will help participants identify the "knowledge gap" between what they know through expertise, research, or lived experience and what a general reader is likely to know. Participants will use that gap to develop a clear, relevant argument for a public audience.Session 3: Editing Your Op-Edwill help participants turn a draft into an accessible, publication-ready piece. Topics will include common word-count requirements, clear and concise language, reducing jargon, checking hyperlinks and sources, anticipating possible misunderstandings, proper image attribution, headline writing, and basic search engine optimization. After the session, participants can send drafts to the instructor for personalized feedback.Session 4: Publishing and Pitching Your Op-Edwill help participants identify the right outlet for their work based on the audience they hope to reach. The session will compare features and challenges of publishing in local and national newspapers, industry publications, institutional blogs, and independent platforms. Participants will learn what to include in a submission or pitch, such as a brief description, author bio, word count, contact information, and headshot, as well as how to recognize potential red flags. The session will conclude with an editor's perspective on what happens behind the inbox, including high submission volume, response times, competition for limited space, and why many submissions may be read without receiving a reply.By the end of the series, participants should understand how to identify a compelling op-ed idea, communicate specialized knowledge to a general audience, edit a piece to common publication standards, and develop a realistic strategy for publication. Participants who work on a piece throughout the program may leave with a completed or near-completed op-ed and a list of appropriate outlets to approach.       Register to attend at https://go.iu.edu/cVZV1S (https://go.iu.edu/cVZV1S) to get the Zoom link.

title: Pie a Cowgirl
description:
The "Pie a Cowgirl" is a fundraising event open to the public for the Western Equestrian Team at IU, with the purpose of raising funds for the team's use. Being an equestrian group, some of our most valuable teammates are our horses, which need round-the-clock care. We are responsible for their health and well-being. We prioritize the entire team learning the basic processes of equine hospitality. We are raising money to help cover some steep costs associated with our non-profit. Horse care costs a lot, including feeding, grooming, vet bills, transportation, and barn boarding, which can be a couple hundred dollars per horse per month. Horse care costs don't include the expenses incurred during the season for the rest of the team. We have other costs, such as travel expenses, competition attire purchases, event food expenses, and more. Having a fundraiser will not only help our team take the required care of our animals and team members, but it will also help us to grow a community of like-minded people who appreciate the environment and wildlife, and expand our relations with other businesses in the future.
We plan to set up a table with pie tins and whipped cream and a few of our exec members who are willing to be pied in the face. The fundraising will be through making the price of each pie-in-the-face a few dollars in cash. 

Hosted by: Western Equestrian at Indiana University

title: Treasures of the Silk Road
location: McCalla Center, McCalla Center, 525 E. 9th Street, Bloomington, IN 47408
description:
The McCalla Center, in collaboration with musician and scholar Shahyar Daneshgar, celebrates the opening of its new exhibition Treasures of the Silk Road on Friday, September 25th, 4:00 pm-6:00 pm EDT.
The exhibit features over 70 musical instruments from the Pastel-Daneshgar musical instrument collection, with a focus on strings, flutes, and percussion from across Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Crafted from wood, snakeskin, horsehair, lambskin, camel bone, and other unique materials, these instruments provide a compelling history of cultural and artistic exchanges that have led to the myriad musical sounds and styles that permeate the world today. The opening event will feature remarks from the collection owner, Shahyar Daneshgar, and will feature musical clips provided by the Lotus World Music & Arts Festival.
Shahyar Daneshgar is a lifelong musician, scholar, and cultural ambassador whose passion for traditional music has shaped more than three decades of collecting, teaching, and performing. Born into a large musical family, he studied at the Tehran Conservatory of Music before pursuing academic work in Germany and later at Indiana University, where he earned his Ph.D. in Central Eurasian Studies in 1995. He taught at Indiana University until his retirement in 2024. He is founder and director of the Bloomington Silk Road Ensemble.
The exhibition is free and runs from September 25, 2026, to September 2027.
The mission of the McCalla Center is to provide accessible exhibition and educational experiences, creating opportunities for students, faculty, and the community to engage with collections, IU-generated creative activity, and community projects in meaningful and innovative ways.

description:
The It’s On Us: Bystander Intervention Workshop is a 90-minute, audience-driven bystander intervention program that teaches students the skills needed to help in situations involving alcohol and drug use that could lead to a sexual assault. Students practice helping in real-life scenarios and discuss how alcohol and drug use influences a person’s ability to give and get consent to engage in sexual activity with another person.  


It's On Us is required for all first-year and transfer undergraduate students. You must attend one session to fulfill the requirement.  


Instructions:  


Those who arrive more than 5 minutes after the start time will NOT be allowed into the session and will need to attend a different session 


If this is your assigned workshop but you cannot attend it in its entirety, please RSVP for a different workshop. 


If you have concerns about attending due to personal experiences or need to request accommodations, please contact the office at itsonus@iu.edu.

description: Oscar-winning documentarians Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor spent three years investigating the technological systems inherent to modern warfare, uncovering their inner workings from the people who designed them. While the revelations uncovered during the film were published in real-time by The Guardian and other outlets over the last three years, the film's power lies in the unvarnished testimony of its participants, letting their own words contextualize their decisions. Students practice helping in real-life scenarios and discuss how alcohol and drug use influences a person’s ability to give and get consent to engage in sexual activity with another person.  


It's On Us is required for all first-year and transfer undergraduate students. You must attend one session to fulfill the requirement.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Healing Art Show 2026 Exhibition
description: Healing Art Show 2026  OPEN OCTOBER 2, 2026 - OCTOBER 30 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM   The Healing Art Show Bloomington is a community art exhibit celebrating the connection between creativity, mental health, and well-being. Inspired by founder & coordinator Juliette Kniola's experience seeing how art became a source of expression, connection, and joy for her sister while navigating mental health challenges, the show was created to bring greater awareness to mental health, normalize conversations about it, and help reduce the stigma that too often surrounds it. First launched in October 2024 in alignment with World Mental Health Day (October 10th), the Healing Art Show has grown into an annual community event supported by local artists, organizations, and partners who believe in the power of art to bring people together.  Now in its third year, the Healing Art Show Bloomington invites artists to share work that reflects the many ways creativity can intersect with mental health and the human experience. Through a diverse collection of artwork, the exhibit creates space for expression, reflection, connection, and moments of joy— while helping people talk more openly about mental health. Each year, more artists and community members become part of the show, helping build a more open, compassionate community where mental health can be discussed without shame or stigma.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: In Search of Freedom: Stories of Afghanistan Exhibition
description: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan  OPEN SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 - DECEMBER 4, 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM  OPEN 5-8 PM ON FIRST FRIDAYS OF THE MONTHIn Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistancelebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural,August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan.Organized in partnership with Indiana University's Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.The exhibition brings together Qahar's vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan's history, traditions, and everyday beauty - withAugust 15: A Mural for Afghanistan,a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. Developed through art therapy workshops with Afghan artists Zainab Ahmadi and Fawzia Abdaly, the mural preserves the participants' voices, memories, hopes, and resilience. The mural stands as a record of collective experience and a tribute to those who continue to seek safety, dignity, and freedom against all odds.Together, the artworks present a deeply human portrait of displacement, resilience, and belonging, inviting visitors to reflect on the the universal connections that unite us across borders, traditions, and generations, and the enduring human desire for freedom.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Osamu James Nakagawa: TRACE | Exhibition
location: FAR Center for Contemporary Arts, 202 S. Rogers St., Bloomington, IN 47404
description: Opening reception and artist talk: Friday, September 4, 58 pm  Nakagawa combines photographs taken at the sites of Japanese-American incarceration camps with photograms of found objects and rubbings of the memorials.  Using diptychs, Nakagawa pairs the past and the present, flattening the boundaries between them. TRACE seeks to reveal what can't be seen anymore, things that happened eighty years ago and have been quietly buried. Through a direct and immersive process, using actual objects and surfaces from the sites, Nakagawa unearths this history of forced incarceration.About the artist:  Osamu James Nakagawa was born in New York City in 1962, raised in Tokyo, and then returned to the US at the age of 15. He is the Distinguished Professor and the Ruth N. Halls Professor of Photography at Indiana University. Nakagawa is a recipient of the 2010 Guggenheim Fellowship, the 2010 Higashikawa New Photographer of the Year and 2015 Sagamihara Photographer of the Year in Japan.  Nakagawa's work has been exhibited internationally, selected solo exhibitions include PGI, Tokyo; Kyoto University of the Arts; Sepia EYE, New York; Sakima Art Museum, Okinawa, Japan; and others. Group shows include "A Shared Elegy" with Emmet Gowin and Elijah Gowin; and "After Photoshop" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. His work is included in numerous public collections, including George Eastman Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum.  Link to the artist's website:https://jamesnakagawa.com/en (https://jamesnakagawa.com/en)  FAR Center for Contemporary Arts:https://thefar.org/events/event/121689 (https://thefar.org/events/event/121689)
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Excursions Into the Weird @ Cultural Arts Gallery
description: "ExcursionsIntothe Weird," is an exhibition of paintings by artist, author, and longtime Bradbury friend John CarterTibbetts, opening October 1 at the Cultural Arts Galleryat IUIndianapolis. Drawing on memories and influences spanning Tibbetts' life, the exhibition traces what he describes as a path away from "the commonplace and the ordinary" and toward the wonderful, extraordinary, and terrifying. The exhibition will remain on view throughout October.Presented as part of Festival451indy.Festival 451indy is sponsored in part by Herbert Simon Family Foundation with additional support from Indiana Humanities

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Samuel Levi Jones: An Archaeology of Knowledge
location: Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University, 1133 E. 7th Street, Fine Arts Plaza, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
For more than a decade, Indiana-born Samuel Levi Jones has created abstract assemblages with found printed and bound matter, deconstructing encyclopedias, law books, medical texts, and other didactic materials. Jones removes their fabric covers and pulps their pages, sewing these swatches together and applying paper pulp to create texturally rich, collaged works with raw edges, loose threads, and worn surfaces. His process of physically destroying archival materials and reconstructing them into artworks constitutes a materially engaged critique of institutional authority, reflecting on systems of knowledge that uphold power and privilege in the United States. For his exhibition at the Eskenazi Museum, Jones mined the museum’s collection for works that resonate with the themes he interrogates, including nationalism and patriotism, censorship, and the representation marginalized identities in historical narratives. Borrowing its title from the ideas of the influential French philosopher Michel Foucault, Samuel Levi Jones: An Archaeology of Knowledge comprises ten years of Jones’ investigations into the underlying structures that shape how we see, speak, and think about culture, politics, and power.
Support for this exhibition has been generously provided by the Robert and Sara LeBien Director's Endowment, Charlie and Jeanetta Nelms, and Janice L. Wiggins.

title: The Photographic Reflex: The Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. Collection
location: Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University, 1133 E. 7th Street, Fine Arts Plaza, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
Spanning more than 150 years, The Photographic Reflex celebrates a transformative gift to the Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University: more than one hundred works by eighty artists, generously donated by Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. This exhibition features photographs dating from 1856 to 2017 and highlights the medium’s extraordinary range, both as a tool for documentation and as a vehicle for artistic exploration.
From Alfred Stieglitz’s delicate studies of grass to Richard Misrach’s vast images of the cosmos, photographers have long found inspiration in the natural world. The built environment has also served as a compelling subject, and the exhibition includes Berenice Abbott’s striking views of 1920s New York City as well as Edward Burtynsky’s sweeping industrial landscapes.
Photography has played a central role in witnessing conflict, from Timothy H. O’Sullivan’s Civil War battlefield to iconic images from World War II, Vietnam, and beyond. While often associated with straightforward depictions of reality, photography also allows artists to experiment with light, exposure, and process to construct imaginative scenes and images beyond human sight.
The Photographic Reflex: The Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. Collection reveals photography’s power to reflect and shape our perception of the world around us across time, space, and vision.
Lead support for this exhibition has been generously provided by the Martha and David Moore Prints, Drawings and Photographs Endowment; Peter and Pamela DePrez; Anne Marks Morgan; Gregory Morse; Efroymson Family Fund; Anne N. DePrez; John J. Medveckis; and Friends of Lee Marks and John DePrez Jr.
Additional support provided by John M. (Jack) Reynolds, Jeffrey A. Wolin, Sandi Clark, and Katherine Campbell and Robert J. Boeglin Jr., M.D.

location: McCalla Center, 525 E. 9th Street, Bloomington, Indiana 47408
description: Outfitting IU Athletics: Hoosier Champions                  This exhibit showcases objects from IU's championship teams and athletes, connecting them to historic achievements in the Big Ten and the national stage. The items featured in the exhibit are from the IU Athletics Sports Memorabilia Collection and feature photos and videos provided by IU Athletics and Indiana University Archives.                Dates: November 14, 2025 - October 2026                                      By Their Own Hands: The Black Filmmakers Hall of Fame!          Founded in 1974 by the Culture and Ethnic Affairs Guild of the Oakland Museum of California, the Black Filmmakers Hall of Fame began as a film lecture series and awards ceremony celebrating achievements of Black film industry figures. When that organization closed, they donated their materials to IU. In collaboration with the IU Black Film Center and Archive, this exhibit features objects from that collection, including founding documents, costumes, and handprints of inductees to the Hall of Fame.        Dates: September 2025 - December 2026                                      Capturing the Campus: T.C. Steele, Indiana University's First Artist in ResidenceCapturing the Campus pays tribute to renowned Hoosier artist T.C. Steele. The exhibit honors the century that has passed since his death by showcasing paintings form the artist's residency at IU and other relevant works. The exhibit will bring together Steele's landscapes from the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection and the Indiana State Museum and Historic Sites' collection, allowing the holdings of these two collections to be viewed in one space.        Dates: April 17, 2026 - April 2026                   Multipurpose Room          Currently Featuring: The Gift of Collecting: Tina Jernigan          Jernigan was a passionate supporter of both Indiana University and the arts. She donated artworks to the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection upon her passing in 2024. With funding provided by Jernigan, Public Art professionally framed, hung, and preserved these pieces for this exhibit in the McCalla Building and for future installations on campus.         Dates: July 2026-July 2027

Before that, she was the Senior Director for China and Taiwan Affairs at the White House National Security Council.This lunch is for graduate and undergraduate students - attendance is capped at the first 25 students to RSVP. Sarah Beran biography: Sarah Beran is president-elect of the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations. She previously served as a partner at Macro Advisory Partners, which she joined in 2025 after a distinguished career in the U.S. Foreign Service — most recently as deputy chief of mission at the U.S. Embassy in Beijing.  From 2022 to 2024, Ms. Beran served as senior director for China and Taiwan Affairs at the White House National Security Council. She led strategic preparations for multiple heads-of-state summits, negotiated the reopening of senior diplomatic channels with Beijing, and helped forge the first U.S.-China understanding on AI safety in the context of nuclear command and control.   Ms. Beran also served as then-U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken's deputy executive secretary for the Indo-Pacific, led the office responsible for U.S. engagement in APEC, and served as former U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo's director of the office of Chinese and Mongolian Affairs. She was posted overseas in Beijing, Islamabad, Jerusalem, and Quito. Her previous domestic assignments include office director for economic policy in the Bureau of East Asian and Pacific Affairs, special assistant to then-Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, and Lebanon desk officer.   Ms. Beran speaks Mandarin and Spanish. She joined the Foreign Service in 2002 and graduated from Claremont McKenna College in 1999.

title: Treasures of the Silk Road
location: McCalla Center, McCalla Center, 525 E. 9th Street, Bloomington, IN 47408
description:
The McCalla Center, in collaboration with musician and scholar Shahyar Daneshgar, celebrates the opening of its new exhibition Treasures of the Silk Road on Friday, September 25th, 4:00 pm-6:00 pm EDT.
The exhibit features over 70 musical instruments from the Pastel-Daneshgar musical instrument collection, with a focus on strings, flutes, and percussion from across Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Crafted from wood, snakeskin, horsehair, lambskin, camel bone, and other unique materials, these instruments provide a compelling history of cultural and artistic exchanges that have led to the myriad musical sounds and styles that permeate the world today. The opening event will feature remarks from the collection owner, Shahyar Daneshgar, and will feature musical clips provided by the Lotus World Music & Arts Festival.
Shahyar Daneshgar is a lifelong musician, scholar, and cultural ambassador whose passion for traditional music has shaped more than three decades of collecting, teaching, and performing. Born into a large musical family, he studied at the Tehran Conservatory of Music before pursuing academic work in Germany and later at Indiana University, where he earned his Ph.D. in Central Eurasian Studies in 1995. He taught at Indiana University until his retirement in 2024. He is founder and director of the Bloomington Silk Road Ensemble.
The exhibition is free and runs from September 25, 2026, to September 2027.
The mission of the McCalla Center is to provide accessible exhibition and educational experiences, creating opportunities for students, faculty, and the community to engage with collections, IU-generated creative activity, and community projects in meaningful and innovative ways.

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Lecture
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound's talk will tease out loose threads in seemingly fixed systems of spatial organization, inviting viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.

title: Everybody to Kenmure Street | Arthouse Now
description: The first day of Eid in Glasgow started as any other. But soon, neighbors heard through community message networks that two local men were snatched up for deportation, and suddenly hundreds of people left their breakfast tables, work Zoom calls, and daily lives to rush down to Kenmure Street to save them by putting their bodies on the line. Though mostly strangers, and with almost no planning, this extremely diverse group organized themselves, taking on essential roles to allow the collective to protect their own from government forces targeting their least protected neighbors. An inspiring and profoundly moving portrait of what we all are capable of in the face of injustice, Everybody to Kenmure Street reminds us of the power that is always inherent in the people. Winner, World Cinema Documentary Special Jury Award for Civil Resistance, Sundance Film Festival 2026. [95 min; documentary; English]

title: Concert Band – Jason H. Nam, conductor – “Of Earth and Sky,” Featuring graduate student conductor Nick Hinman
location: Musical Arts Center, 101 N Eagleson Ave, Bloomington, IN 47406
description:
Enjoy this performance from almost anywhere in the world via LIVE@jacobs!
Repertoire
Steven Bryant: In This Broad Earth (2015)
Joni Greene: Splitting Light (2026, consortium premiere)
Gala Flagello: Love and Nature (2024)
Aaron Perrine: Pale Blue on Deep (2011)
Dana Wilson: Colorado Peaks (2005)
John Mackey: Aurora Awakes (2009)
About the Conductor
Jason H. Nam is associate professor of music in bands at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music, where he conducts bands and teaches undergraduate and graduate courses in instrumental conducting, administration of school bands, and wind literature. Nam earned a Doctor of Music in Wind Conducting degree from the Jacobs School, where he studied with Stephen W. Pratt. He earned an M.M. in Conducting and a B.M. in Music Education from the University of Redlands, where he studied with Eddie R. Smith. Nam served as a lecturer in the Department of Music at California State University, San Bernardino, and as director of bands at La Colina Junior High School and San Marcos High School in Santa Barbara, California. More recently, he has served as a faculty member, ensemble conductor, and director of the IU Summer Music Clinic. Nam keeps a busy schedule as conductor, adjudicator, and clinician across North America. He was named a national finalist for The American Prize in Conducting (Band/Wind Ensemble division) in 2017 amd 2023. His IU Concert Band was invited to perform at the 2020 College Band Directors National Association North Central Conference in Chicago, Illinois. Nam served as resident music director of the Bloomington-based Southern Indiana Wind Ensemble from 2016 to 2021, performing widely throughout Indiana and as an invited ensemble at the Ohio Music Educators Professional Development Conference in 2020. He has been published in the Journal of the National Band Association and the American Bandmasters Association’s Journal of Band Research. His research interests include the music of William Bolcom, the wind chamber music of Igor Stravinsky, the historical development of the wind band repertoire in the twentieth century, and effective rehearsal methodologies for conductors. Nam currently serves on the national selection committee for the National Band Association/William D. Revelli Memorial Band Composition Contest and holds professional memberships in the College Band Directors National Association, National Band Association, Conductors Guild, Indiana Music Education Association, and Pi Kappa Lambda music honor society.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.

title: Healing Art Show 2026 Exhibition
description: Healing Art Show 2026  OPEN OCTOBER 2, 2026 - OCTOBER 30 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM   The Healing Art Show Bloomington is a community art exhibit celebrating the connection between creativity, mental health, and well-being. Inspired by founder & coordinator Juliette Kniola's experience seeing how art became a source of expression, connection, and joy for her sister while navigating mental health challenges, the show was created to bring greater awareness to mental health, normalize conversations about it, and help reduce the stigma that too often surrounds it. First launched in October 2024 in alignment with World Mental Health Day (October 10th), the Healing Art Show has grown into an annual community event supported by local artists, organizations, and partners who believe in the power of art to bring people together.  Now in its third year, the Healing Art Show Bloomington invites artists to share work that reflects the many ways creativity can intersect with mental health and the human experience. Through a diverse collection of artwork, the exhibit creates space for expression, reflection, connection, and moments of joy— while helping people talk more openly about mental health. Each year, more artists and community members become part of the show, helping build a more open, compassionate community where mental health can be discussed without shame or stigma.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: In Search of Freedom: Stories of Afghanistan Exhibition
description: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan  OPEN SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 - DECEMBER 4, 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM  OPEN 5-8 PM ON FIRST FRIDAYS OF THE MONTHIn Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistancelebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural,August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan.Organized in partnership with Indiana University's Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.The exhibition brings together Qahar's vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan's history, traditions, and everyday beauty - withAugust 15: A Mural for Afghanistan,a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. Developed through art therapy workshops with Afghan artists Zainab Ahmadi and Fawzia Abdaly, the mural preserves the participants' voices, memories, hopes, and resilience. The mural stands as a record of collective experience and a tribute to those who continue to seek safety, dignity, and freedom against all odds.Together, the artworks present a deeply human portrait of displacement, resilience, and belonging, inviting visitors to reflect on the the universal connections that unite us across borders, traditions, and generations, and the enduring human desire for freedom.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Osamu James Nakagawa: TRACE | Exhibition
location: FAR Center for Contemporary Arts, 202 S. Rogers St., Bloomington, IN 47404
description: Opening reception and artist talk: Friday, September 4, 58 pm  Nakagawa combines photographs taken at the sites of Japanese-American incarceration camps with photograms of found objects and rubbings of the memorials.  Using diptychs, Nakagawa pairs the past and the present, flattening the boundaries between them. TRACE seeks to reveal what can't be seen anymore, things that happened eighty years ago and have been quietly buried. Through a direct and immersive process, using actual objects and surfaces from the sites, Nakagawa unearths this history of forced incarceration.About the artist:  Osamu James Nakagawa was born in New York City in 1962, raised in Tokyo, and then returned to the US at the age of 15. He is the Distinguished Professor and the Ruth N. Halls Professor of Photography at Indiana University. Nakagawa is a recipient of the 2010 Guggenheim Fellowship, the 2010 Higashikawa New Photographer of the Year and 2015 Sagamihara Photographer of the Year in Japan.  Nakagawa's work has been exhibited internationally, selected solo exhibitions include PGI, Tokyo; Kyoto University of the Arts; Sepia EYE, New York; Sakima Art Museum, Okinawa, Japan; and others. Group shows include "A Shared Elegy" with Emmet Gowin and Elijah Gowin; and "After Photoshop" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. His work is included in numerous public collections, including George Eastman Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum.  Link to the artist's website:https://jamesnakagawa.com/en (https://jamesnakagawa.com/en)  FAR Center for Contemporary Arts:https://thefar.org/events/event/121689 (https://thefar.org/events/event/121689)
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

description: "ExcursionsIntothe Weird," is an exhibition of paintings by artist, author, and longtime Bradbury friend John CarterTibbetts, opening October 1 at the Cultural Arts Galleryat IUIndianapolis. Drawing on memories and influences spanning Tibbetts' life, the exhibition traces what he describes as a path away from "the commonplace and the ordinary" and toward the wonderful, extraordinary, and terrifying. title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.

title: Samuel Levi Jones: An Archaeology of Knowledge
location: Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University, 1133 E. 7th Street, Fine Arts Plaza, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
For more than a decade, Indiana-born Samuel Levi Jones has created abstract assemblages with found printed and bound matter, deconstructing encyclopedias, law books, medical texts, and other didactic materials. Jones removes their fabric covers and pulps their pages, sewing these swatches together and applying paper pulp to create texturally rich, collaged works with raw edges, loose threads, and worn surfaces. His process of physically destroying archival materials and reconstructing them into artworks constitutes a materially engaged critique of institutional authority, reflecting on systems of knowledge that uphold power and privilege in the United States. For his exhibition at the Eskenazi Museum, Jones mined the museum’s collection for works that resonate with the themes he interrogates, including nationalism and patriotism, censorship, and the representation marginalized identities in historical narratives. Borrowing its title from the ideas of the influential French philosopher Michel Foucault, Samuel Levi Jones: An Archaeology of Knowledge comprises ten years of Jones’ investigations into the underlying structures that shape how we see, speak, and think about culture, politics, and power.
Support for this exhibition has been generously provided by the Robert and Sara LeBien Director's Endowment, Charlie and Jeanetta Nelms, and Janice L. Wiggins.

title: The Photographic Reflex: The Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. Collection
location: Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University, 1133 E. 7th Street, Fine Arts Plaza, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
Spanning more than 150 years, The Photographic Reflex celebrates a transformative gift to the Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University: more than one hundred works by eighty artists, generously donated by Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. This exhibition features photographs dating from 1856 to 2017 and highlights the medium’s extraordinary range, both as a tool for documentation and as a vehicle for artistic exploration.
From Alfred Stieglitz’s delicate studies of grass to Richard Misrach’s vast images of the cosmos, photographers have long found inspiration in the natural world. The built environment has also served as a compelling subject, and the exhibition includes Berenice Abbott’s striking views of 1920s New York City as well as Edward Burtynsky’s sweeping industrial landscapes.
Photography has played a central role in witnessing conflict, from Timothy H. O’Sullivan’s Civil War battlefield to iconic images from World War II, Vietnam, and beyond. While often associated with straightforward depictions of reality, photography also allows artists to experiment with light, exposure, and process to construct imaginative scenes and images beyond human sight.
The Photographic Reflex: The Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. Collection reveals photography’s power to reflect and shape our perception of the world around us across time, space, and vision.
Lead support for this exhibition has been generously provided by the Martha and David Moore Prints, Drawings and Photographs Endowment; Peter and Pamela DePrez; Anne Marks Morgan; Gregory Morse; Efroymson Family Fund; Anne N. DePrez; John J. Medveckis; and Friends of Lee Marks and John DePrez Jr.
Additional support provided by John M. (Jack) Reynolds, Jeffrey A. Wolin, Sandi Clark, and Katherine Campbell and Robert J. Boeglin Jr., M.D.

description: Outfitting IU Athletics: Hoosier Champions                  This exhibit showcases objects from IU's championship teams and athletes, connecting them to historic achievements in the Big Ten and the national stage. The items featured in the exhibit are from the IU Athletics Sports Memorabilia Collection and feature photos and videos provided by IU Athletics and Indiana University Archives.                Dates: November 14, 2025 - October 2026                                      By Their Own Hands: The Black Filmmakers Hall of Fame!          Founded in 1974 by the Culture and Ethnic Affairs Guild of the Oakland Museum of California, the Black Filmmakers Hall of Fame began as a film lecture series and awards ceremony celebrating achievements of Black film industry figures. When that organization closed, they donated their materials to IU. In collaboration with the IU Black Film Center and Archive, this exhibit features objects from that collection, including founding documents, costumes, and handprints of inductees to the Hall of Fame.        Dates: September 2025 - December 2026                                      Capturing the Campus: T.C. Steele, Indiana University's First Artist in ResidenceCapturing the Campus pays tribute to renowned Hoosier artist T.C. Steele. The exhibit honors the century that has passed since his death by showcasing paintings form the artist's residency at IU and other relevant works. The exhibit will bring together Steele's landscapes from the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection and the Indiana State Museum and Historic Sites' collection, allowing the holdings of these two collections to be viewed in one space.        Dates: April 17, 2026 - April 2026                   Multipurpose Room          Currently Featuring: The Gift of Collecting: Tina Jernigan          Jernigan was a passionate supporter of both Indiana University and the arts. She donated artworks to the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection upon her passing in 2024. title: Beginning Watercolor
location: Ivy Tech Community College Bloomington (Center for Lifelong Learning), 200 Daniels Way, Bloomington, Indiana 47404
description:
This introductory watercolor class with award-winning artist and instructor, Mary Sue Veerkamp Schwab, is packed full of helpful information for beginner level students. Whether you paint along with the instructor or work on your own, you can expect individual attention and will be amazed at what you can do! 
 Class Objectives:
- Review of the basics: What can my brushes and paper do for me?
- Wet-on-Wet: Applying wet paint to a pre wetted paper to create a soft blend for skies and florals. 
- Wet-on-Dry: Applying paint directly to dry paper for a sharp controlled edge. 
- Layering watercolor with watercolor (transparent washes) 
- Use layering and dry brush on small compositions to hone skills 
 This class will include demonstrations and students participate in supportive classroom critiques. Many students request taking this class a second or third time! 
 Supplies: The following materials are based on Mary Sue's painting approach, and are suggestions, not requirements. Students are welcome to incorporate their own material preferences, and must bring their own supplies:
 Paper:
The most important element. Arches cold press paper is recommended, in block or sheet formats.
- Block, 140pound, Cold Press, 9x12 or 10 x14 or 11x14.
- Large individual sheets, can be divided into 2-4 smaller sheets, buy Cold Press.
 Paints:
I recommend a limited palette. 10 Winsor & Newton Professional grade colors:
- 6 warm colors: Winsor Red, Winsor Yellow, Burnt Siena, and Raw Siena, Permanent Rose and Winsor Violet.
- 4 cool colors: Winsor Blue Green Shade, Winsor Blue Red Shade, Hookers Green, and Paynes Grey.
 Other items:
- Dr. Ph. Martin's Bleed Proof White Fine Art Paint, or similar opaque white.
- Pencils, hard lead 2H or 4H
- *Pencil sharpener
- Kneaded eraser
- *Drawing board, 12"x26"
- White watercolor tape (not painter's tape)
- Palette and mixing pans (preferred is ceramic white palette)
- *2 small water holders or cups
- Small mixing pans for colors, mine have lids.
*Drawing boards, pencil sharpener, paper towels, rulers, and water holders/cups will be available, but you may use your own if preferred.
 Brushes:
Do not spend a fortune on brushes. Winsor & Newton has an inexpensive line. I also like the black silver brushes.
Sizes: 1” and ½”flat; #4 or #7 #10 round; Detail #2 round. Must have a couple of large watercolor brushes for washes. My favorite brush: Silver Black Velvet Oval ¾”.
 Supplies can be ordered from several art suppliers including Blick, Jerry's Artarama, or Bloomington Fine Arts Supply if you prefer to shop locally.

title: Ostrom Workshop | Research Series: Camilo Rey-Sabogal
location: The Ostrom Workshop, 513 N PARK AVE
description: Bio  Dr. Camilo Rey-Sabogal is an Associate Professor at the Faculty of Social Sciences and Education, Universidad de Cartagena, Colombia. He investigates the political economy of urban space, focusing on how territorial transformations shape access to housing, work, and rights for vulnerable populations. His research examines residential segregation, migration, gentrification, housing policy and urban inequalities, with sustained fieldwork in Cartagena and the Colombian Caribbean.Title  Land Scarcity and Flood-Risk Zoning: How Tourism Gentrification and Climate Change Limit Affordable Housing in CartagenaAbstract  Over the past two decades, Cartagena has undergone major housing market transformations driven by tourism-driven real estate speculation, the financialization of housing, climate-driven flooding risks, and migration pressures. This research examines how tourism gentrification and the reduction of buildable land due to flood risk jointly constrain affordable housing production in Cartagena, and identifies institutional arrangements capable of improving the governance of scarce, secure urban land under conditions of real estate pressure and climate vulnerability.  The study employs a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative spatial analysis of housing price dynamics across urban submarkets, multi-layered vulnerability mapping, and institutional analysis of planning mechanisms. It addresses three core questions: (1) How do tourism-driven gentrification dynamics generate ripple effects across housing submarkets that reduce the availability and affordability of social housing? (2) How do climate-related flood risks exacerbate land scarcity and affect vulnerable households' access to housing? (3) What institutional arrangements and governance mechanisms could reduce the social housing deficit in contexts shaped by real estate pressure and climate risk?About the Ostrom Workshop Research Series  Learn about innovative research by Graduate Students and Visiting Scholars as they advance the mission of the Ostrom Workshop, building upon the theme of governance to understand and address major societal problems.

title: Treasures of the Silk Road
location: McCalla Center, McCalla Center, 525 E. 9th Street, Bloomington, IN 47408
description:
The McCalla Center, in collaboration with musician and scholar Shahyar Daneshgar, celebrates the opening of its new exhibition Treasures of the Silk Road on Friday, September 25th, 4:00 pm-6:00 pm EDT.
The exhibit features over 70 musical instruments from the Pastel-Daneshgar musical instrument collection, with a focus on strings, flutes, and percussion from across Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Crafted from wood, snakeskin, horsehair, lambskin, camel bone, and other unique materials, these instruments provide a compelling history of cultural and artistic exchanges that have led to the myriad musical sounds and styles that permeate the world today. The opening event will feature remarks from the collection owner, Shahyar Daneshgar, and will feature musical clips provided by the Lotus World Music & Arts Festival.
Shahyar Daneshgar is a lifelong musician, scholar, and cultural ambassador whose passion for traditional music has shaped more than three decades of collecting, teaching, and performing. Born into a large musical family, he studied at the Tehran Conservatory of Music before pursuing academic work in Germany and later at Indiana University, where he earned his Ph.D. in Central Eurasian Studies in 1995. He taught at Indiana University until his retirement in 2024. He is founder and director of the Bloomington Silk Road Ensemble.
The exhibition is free and runs from September 25, 2026, to September 2027.
The mission of the McCalla Center is to provide accessible exhibition and educational experiences, creating opportunities for students, faculty, and the community to engage with collections, IU-generated creative activity, and community projects in meaningful and innovative ways.

Symphonic Band – Eric M. Smedley, conductor
description: Enjoy this performance from almost anywhere in the world viaLIVE@jacobs!Repertoire  Joseph Turrin: Academy Overture (2017)Benson: The Leaves are Falling (1964)Corey Chang: What's Next? (2024/25, premiere, D.M. dissertation)Joni Greene: AfterGlow (2024)Jodie Blackshaw: 22° halo (2022)Alfred Reed: Russian Christmas Music (1944/69)About the ConductorEric M. Smedley is associate professor of music in bands at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music, where he directs the Symphonic Band, teaches undergraduate and graduate instrumental conducting courses, and serves as the director of the Big Red Basketball Band. Smedley earned a Doctor of Musical Arts degree from the University of Washington and Master of Music and Bachelor of Music Education degrees from the Jacobs School of Music. He previously served on the music faculties of Boise State University and Western Kentucky University and as a public-school music educator in Cocoa Beach, Florida; Santa Monica, California; and Kenosha, Wisconsin. He has conducted throughout North America and in Vietnam, Poland, Russia, and Japan. Smedley maintains an active schedule as a clinician, guest conductor, adjudicator, and trumpet performer. His Symphonic Band was selected to perform at the 2018 College Band Directors National Association North Central Conference. He was a finalist at the 2023 Warsaw Wind Band Conducting Competition in Warsaw, Poland. In 2025, Navona Records released the album Origins and Expansions, featuring a composition by Kevin Bobo, world-renowned steel pan soloist Liam Teague, and the IU Wind Ensemble. Smedley's research interests are varied and include projects in the areas of contemporary wind band literature, wind band orchestration, and conducting pedagogy. Smedley is a member of the Gamma chapter of the international band fraternity Phi Beta Mu and is an honorary member of Kappa Kappa Psi, Tau Beta Sigma, and Phi Mu Alpha Sinfonia. He is a member of the College Band Directors National Association and the National Association for Music Education. He lives in Bloomington, Indiana, with his wife, Jessica, their daughter, Ella, and their Bedlington Terriers, Piper and Finn. Meeting URL: https://liveatjacobs.music.indiana.edu/

title: Chi Ho Han, piano
description: Enjoy this performance from almost anywhere in the world viaLIVE@jacobs!Repertoire  R. Schumann: Fantasie in C Major, Op. 17 (1838)Liszt : Sonata in B Minor, S.178 (1853)About the Artist  South Korean concert pianist Chi Ho Han is associate professor of music in piano at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. He is an artist with an unmistakable personal mark, embracing technical diversity, emotional realness, and philosophical depth in all his unique recital programs. Establishing a firm conviction in German arts at age 20, he received top prizes at Beethoven competitions in Vienna and Bonn and a Schubert competition in Dortmund. Earlier achievements include first prize and the Audience Award at the International Kissinger KlavierOlymp Competition (Germany, 2013), first prize at the Seoul International Music Competition (Korea, 2014), top prize at the ARD International Music Competition with additional Audience Award and Best Performance on Commissioned Work (Germany, 2014), silver medal at the Gina Bachauer International Artists Piano Competition (United States, 2014), and fourth prize at the Queen Elisabeth International Competition (Belgium, 2016). He was awarded third prize and the Isang Yun Prize at the Orléans International Piano Competition on contemporary art music (France, 2022). Han was artist-in-residence at the Korean Cultural Centre in Budapest from 2022 to 2023 and performed to critical acclaim at the Seoul Arts Center Symphony Festival, Festival Internazionale di Musica da Camera di Cervo, International Klavier-Festival Ruhr, Kissinger Sommer International Music Festival, International Rheingau Music Festival, International Bodensee Music Festival, Lake Como Piano Festival, Musikdorf Ernen, and Deer Valley Music Festival. Han has performed worldwide, including the complete Beethoven concertos, Romantic and Russian standards to contemporary commissions, collaborations with the Austrian Radio Symphony Orchestra, Bavarian Radio Symphony Orchestra, National Orchestra of Belgium, Lviv National Philharmonic, Munich Chamber Orchestra, Philharmonic Orchestra of Marseille, Seoul Philharmonic Orchestra, and St. Petersburg Symphony Orchestra. He is a protégé of pianist-composer György Kurtág and a former student of Arnulf von Arnim and Arie Vardi. "He plays the way great composers themselves would have played," said Kurtág of Han in Budapest in 2023. Meeting URL: https://liveatjacobs.music.indiana.edu/
source: IU Jacobs School of Music, WFIU Community Calendar

title: Open Mic Night at The Comedy Attic
location: The Comedy Attic,123 S Walnut St, Bloomington, IN 47408, USA
description:
Every Wednesday at 8PM is Comedy Attic Open Mic Night. Bloomington has one of the best local comedy scenes in the country, and it all starts with our open mic night!

Each comedian is asked to do no more than five minutes of completely original material. While we do not care about foul language in your set, we do not allow racist, homophobic, transphobic or rape/female bashing jokes. If you have to ask if it's racist, homophobic, transphobic or a rape joke, it probably is.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.
