title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: In Search of Freedom: Stories of Afghanistan Exhibition
description: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan  OPEN SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 - DECEMBER 4, 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM  OPEN 5-8 PM ON FIRST FRIDAYS OF THE MONTHIn Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistancelebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural,August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan.Organized in partnership with Indiana University's Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.The exhibition brings together Qahar's vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan's history, traditions, and everyday beauty - withAugust 15: A Mural for Afghanistan,a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. Developed through art therapy workshops with Afghan artists Zainab Ahmadi and Fawzia Abdaly, the mural preserves the participants' voices, memories, hopes, and resilience. The mural stands as a record of collective experience and a tribute to those who continue to seek safety, dignity, and freedom against all odds.Together, the artworks present a deeply human portrait of displacement, resilience, and belonging, inviting visitors to reflect on the the universal connections that unite us across borders, traditions, and generations, and the enduring human desire for freedom.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Samuel Levi Jones: An Archaeology of Knowledge
location: Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University, 1133 E. 7th Street, Fine Arts Plaza, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
For more than a decade, Indiana-born Samuel Levi Jones has created abstract assemblages with found printed and bound matter, deconstructing encyclopedias, law books, medical texts, and other didactic materials. Jones removes their fabric covers and pulps their pages, sewing these swatches together and applying paper pulp to create texturally rich, collaged works with raw edges, loose threads, and worn surfaces. His process of physically destroying archival materials and reconstructing them into artworks constitutes a materially engaged critique of institutional authority, reflecting on systems of knowledge that uphold power and privilege in the United States. For his exhibition at the Eskenazi Museum, Jones mined the museum’s collection for works that resonate with the themes he interrogates, including nationalism and patriotism, censorship, and the representation marginalized identities in historical narratives. Borrowing its title from the ideas of the influential French philosopher Michel Foucault, Samuel Levi Jones: An Archaeology of Knowledge comprises ten years of Jones’ investigations into the underlying structures that shape how we see, speak, and think about culture, politics, and power.
Support for this exhibition has been generously provided by the Robert and Sara LeBien Director's Endowment, Charlie and Jeanetta Nelms, and Janice L. Wiggins.

title: The Photographic Reflex: The Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. Collection
location: Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University, 1133 E. 7th Street, Fine Arts Plaza, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
Spanning more than 150 years, The Photographic Reflex celebrates a transformative gift to the Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University: more than one hundred works by eighty artists, generously donated by Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. This exhibition features photographs dating from 1856 to 2017 and highlights the medium’s extraordinary range, both as a tool for documentation and as a vehicle for artistic exploration.
From Alfred Stieglitz’s delicate studies of grass to Richard Misrach’s vast images of the cosmos, photographers have long found inspiration in the natural world. The built environment has also served as a compelling subject, and the exhibition includes Berenice Abbott’s striking views of 1920s New York City as well as Edward Burtynsky’s sweeping industrial landscapes.
Photography has played a central role in witnessing conflict, from Timothy H. O’Sullivan’s Civil War battlefield to iconic images from World War II, Vietnam, and beyond. While often associated with straightforward depictions of reality, photography also allows artists to experiment with light, exposure, and process to construct imaginative scenes and images beyond human sight.
The Photographic Reflex: The Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. Collection reveals photography’s power to reflect and shape our perception of the world around us across time, space, and vision.
Lead support for this exhibition has been generously provided by the Martha and David Moore Prints, Drawings and Photographs Endowment; Peter and Pamela DePrez; Anne Marks Morgan; Gregory Morse; Efroymson Family Fund; Anne N. DePrez; John J. Medveckis; and Friends of Lee Marks and John DePrez Jr.
Additional support provided by John M. (Jack) Reynolds, Jeffrey A. Wolin, Sandi Clark, and Katherine Campbell and Robert J. Boeglin Jr., M.D.

Mike Mattner, clarinet; Kimberly Carballo, piano
description: Featuring  Eric Bowling, flute (alumnus guest)  Jacob Burk, violaSara Dailey, narrator (alumna guest) Helen Ford, cello (guest)  Michael Grubb, narrator (guest)  Maria Izzo, soprano (alumna guest)  Emily Nehus, violin (alumna guest)  Paulina Villarreal, mezzo-soprano/narrator  RepertoireChappell Kingsland: Confessions of a Murderess (2011)Anthony Plog: Animal Ditties I (1978)Daniel Cueto: Ave (2025)Elaine Fine: Happy Family (2005)Jenni Brandon: The Woman with the Unfathomable Eyes (2010)About the Artists  Clarinetist Mike Mattner (M.M. University of Colorado, Boulder; B.Mus.Ed. Crane School of Music-SUNY Potsdam) has enjoyed a teaching and performing career spanning 34 years. He is a former member of the Midland Symphony, Boulder MahlerFest Orchestra, Philharmonia à Vent, Orion Winds, Bloomington Pops, Bloomington Symphony, Class Act Productions, Houston Repertoire Ballet, The Woodlands Concert Band, and the Woodland Winds Quintet, and has performed in numerous musical theater productions. He currently performs with the Bloomington Symphony Orchestra, the Southern Indiana Wind Ensemble, Reimagining Opera for Kids, Voces Novae, and several chamber music ensembles.Kimberly Carballo serves in the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music as Director of Jacobs Virtual Academy (JVA) and as teaching professor in the Chamber Music and Collaborative Piano department. Carballo is also an active international performer and educator, teaching both at the university and in her private studio. She is a strong believer in and practicer of community engagement locally and globally. She founded Reimagining Opera for Kids (ROK), a music Bloomington-based community engagement and education program, participates annually as faculty advisor for the IU portion of the team in the Cheerful Heart Music Education Mission in the Dominican Republic and Haiti, and is a founding member of the Amity Trio, a chamber ensemble that commissions and performs new music to amplify underrepresented voices.

title: Hotel California – The Original Eagles Tribute
description:
For over three decades now **HOTEL CALIFORNIA** have been recreating the legendary sound of **The Eagles**, and thrilling audiences all over the world. From the quintessential Eagles anthem “**Hotel California**” thru “**Take It Easy**”, “**Lyin’ Eyes**”, “**Take It to the Limit**”, “**Peaceful Easy Feeling**”, “**One of These Nights**”, “**Dirty Laundry**”, “**Already Gone**”, “**The Long Run**”, “**Life In the Fast Lane**” and “**Desperado**”, they have evolved into a masterful celebration of **The Eagles**’ music.

The band set the bar in 1986, and they’ve remained the industry leading substitute for **The Eagles** ever since. Playing to huge outdoor and arena audiences, sharing bills with some of rock’s legends, and going places no tribute band has gone before. A long run by any measure, but it begs the question – what makes **HOTEL CALIFORNIA** so special?

Simply put, incredible lead vocal similarity, intensely accurate instrumental work, soaring harmonies, and top-flight live performances, just for starters. These are the band’s hallmarks, and the foundation on which their reputation has been built. With over a century of collective professional experience in the band today, they’re still going stronger than ever!

If you love **The Eagles**, then welcome to the **HOTEL CALIFORNIA** – you’ve just found the next-best thing.

description: Enjoy this performance from almost anywhere in the world viaLIVE@jacobs!Repertoire  Rossini: Petite messe solennelleAbout the ConductorBetsy Burleigh is Thomas R. Kasdorf Professor of Choral Conducting and professor of music at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music, where she was chair of the Choral Conducting Department from 2013 to 2024. Burleigh served as music director of the Mendelssohn Choir of Pittsburgh from 2006 to 2015, leading performances of Brahms' Requiem, Bach's B Minor Mass, Rachmaninoff's All-Night Vigil, and Mozart's Great Mass in C Minor, and preparing the choir for performances with the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra (PSO). As a guest conductor, Burleigh has led the PSO, Rhode Island Philharmonic, Akron Symphony, Canton Symphony, and Handel Society of Dartmouth College. She prepared the Tanglewood Festival Chorus for performances with the Boston Symphony Orchestra and the Cincinnati May Festival Chorus for performances with the Cincinnati Pops. Burleigh served as assistant director of The Cleveland Orchestra Chorus for 11 years, during which time she prepared the chorus for all performances at the Blossom Festival and oversaw the chorus for Pierre Boulez's Deutsche Gramophone recording of Berlioz's Roméo et Juliette. Other positions have included directing the Providence Singers, Akron Symphony Chorus, Canton Symphony Chorus, and Mastersingers of Lexington. Acclaimed for her oratorio conducting, Burleigh's Chorus pro Musica performance of Haydn's Creation was praised as an "expansive, poetic reading" (The Boston Globe). Her rendition of Orff's Carmina Burana was called both "nuanced" and "hair-raising" (The Boston Musical Intelligencer). She won the 2000 Northern Ohio Live Achievement Award for best classical/opera performance for Ulmann's Der Kaiser von Atlantis and conducted The Cleveland Orchestra Chorus on an Emmy Award-winning concert for the 9/11 Red Cross Disaster Relief Fund. Burleigh previously held teaching positions at Tufts, Clark, Southeastern Massachusetts, and Cleveland State universities, Longy School of Music, and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. She earned a Bachelor of Music Education degree with distinction from Indiana University, a Master of Music in Choral Conducting degree with distinction from the New England Conservatory of Music, and a Doctor of Music in Choral Conducting from the Jacobs School. title: Blue October
description:
Twenty years after the album that launched them into the global spotlight, Blue October celebrates the anniversary of their platinum-selling record Foiled with a global tour including a return to the Brown County Music Center in Nashville, Ind., on Sunday, November 8, 2026. The band will also release a special vinyl reissue, arriving May 29 via Universal Music.
Blue October’s deeply personal songwriting and emotionally resonant sound on Foiled cemented the Houston-bred band as one of rock’s most distinctive voices. While Foiled marked a breakthrough moment for the band, it was only the beginning. Its impact continues to ripple  outward as new listeners discover the album alongside the expansive catalog that followed. The  connection forged through its lyrics has only deepened over time, helping grow a devoted global audience. Blue October’s catalog now surpasses one billion streams and continues to climb.
The album initially sent frontman Justin Furstenfeld and Blue October’s life into a whirlwind,  now, as the singer looks back on it 20 years in the rearview, and particularly as the band prepares  to launch a yearlong Foiled 20th-anniversary celebration, he has come to realize what a true  blessing his band’s most beloved body of work has been in his life. Furstenfeld wrote the songs during an intensely personal period while living alone in Los Angeles,  first capturing them as raw demos that reflected the vulnerability behind the record. Produced by  Furstenfeld and David Castell, the 14-track collection balances deeply confessional lyrics with  soaring melodies and emotional honesty that became a hallmark.
Cracking the Billboard Rock Chart Top 10, Foiled remains a cornerstone of alternative rock,  anchored by Billboard-charting hits, including the platinum-certified “Hate Me,” “Into the Ocean” and fan favorite “She’s My Ride Home.”

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: In Search of Freedom: Stories of Afghanistan Exhibition
description: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan  OPEN SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 - DECEMBER 4, 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM  OPEN 5-8 PM ON FIRST FRIDAYS OF THE MONTHIn Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistancelebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural,August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan.Organized in partnership with Indiana University's Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.The exhibition brings together Qahar's vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan's history, traditions, and everyday beauty - withAugust 15: A Mural for Afghanistan,a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. Developed through art therapy workshops with Afghan artists Zainab Ahmadi and Fawzia Abdaly, the mural preserves the participants' voices, memories, hopes, and resilience. The mural stands as a record of collective experience and a tribute to those who continue to seek safety, dignity, and freedom against all odds.Together, the artworks present a deeply human portrait of displacement, resilience, and belonging, inviting visitors to reflect on the the universal connections that unite us across borders, traditions, and generations, and the enduring human desire for freedom.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Samuel Levi Jones: An Archaeology of Knowledge
location: Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University, 1133 E. 7th Street, Fine Arts Plaza, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
For more than a decade, Indiana-born Samuel Levi Jones has created abstract assemblages with found printed and bound matter, deconstructing encyclopedias, law books, medical texts, and other didactic materials. Jones removes their fabric covers and pulps their pages, sewing these swatches together and applying paper pulp to create texturally rich, collaged works with raw edges, loose threads, and worn surfaces. His process of physically destroying archival materials and reconstructing them into artworks constitutes a materially engaged critique of institutional authority, reflecting on systems of knowledge that uphold power and privilege in the United States. For his exhibition at the Eskenazi Museum, Jones mined the museum’s collection for works that resonate with the themes he interrogates, including nationalism and patriotism, censorship, and the representation marginalized identities in historical narratives. Borrowing its title from the ideas of the influential French philosopher Michel Foucault, Samuel Levi Jones: An Archaeology of Knowledge comprises ten years of Jones’ investigations into the underlying structures that shape how we see, speak, and think about culture, politics, and power.
Support for this exhibition has been generously provided by the Robert and Sara LeBien Director's Endowment, Charlie and Jeanetta Nelms, and Janice L. Wiggins.

title: The Photographic Reflex: The Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. Collection
location: Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University, 1133 E. 7th Street, Fine Arts Plaza, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
Spanning more than 150 years, The Photographic Reflex celebrates a transformative gift to the Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University: more than one hundred works by eighty artists, generously donated by Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. This exhibition features photographs dating from 1856 to 2017 and highlights the medium’s extraordinary range, both as a tool for documentation and as a vehicle for artistic exploration.
From Alfred Stieglitz’s delicate studies of grass to Richard Misrach’s vast images of the cosmos, photographers have long found inspiration in the natural world. The built environment has also served as a compelling subject, and the exhibition includes Berenice Abbott’s striking views of 1920s New York City as well as Edward Burtynsky’s sweeping industrial landscapes.
Photography has played a central role in witnessing conflict, from Timothy H. O’Sullivan’s Civil War battlefield to iconic images from World War II, Vietnam, and beyond. While often associated with straightforward depictions of reality, photography also allows artists to experiment with light, exposure, and process to construct imaginative scenes and images beyond human sight.
The Photographic Reflex: The Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. Collection reveals photography’s power to reflect and shape our perception of the world around us across time, space, and vision.
Lead support for this exhibition has been generously provided by the Martha and David Moore Prints, Drawings and Photographs Endowment; Peter and Pamela DePrez; Anne Marks Morgan; Gregory Morse; Efroymson Family Fund; Anne N. DePrez; John J. Medveckis; and Friends of Lee Marks and John DePrez Jr.
Additional support provided by John M. (Jack) Reynolds, Jeffrey A. Wolin, Sandi Clark, and Katherine Campbell and Robert J. Boeglin Jr., M.D.

title: ACES Horizon Talk: ""The Soviet Factor in China's Regional Ethnic Autonomy: A Sino-Soviet Comparison of Institutions and Ethnic Elites." by Dr. Jun Kumakura
description: Since the founding of the Chinese Communist Party in the 1920s, the Party advocated the idea of a federal state under the influence of the Soviet Union. In 1949, however, shortly before the founding of the People's Republic of China, the CCP turned toward a form of state-building different from federalism and adopted regional ethnic autonomy. While this shift is often understood as reflecting China's distinctive approach to state-building, the Soviet dimension—including Stalin's apparent acceptance of the CCP's decision—has received comparatively little attention.  Drawing on research developed from his doctoral dissertation, Professor Jun Kumakura examines the Soviet influence on the CCP's system of regional ethnic autonomy and traces the subsequent divergence between Chinese and Soviet policies toward ethnic elites.Date & Time:  Monday, November 9  12:00 PM – 1:30 PMLocation:  GISB 1060This talk will be held in person only. Lunch will be provided. title: Treasures of the Silk Road
location: McCalla Center, McCalla Center, 525 E. 9th Street, Bloomington, IN 47408
description:
The McCalla Center, in collaboration with musician and scholar Shahyar Daneshgar, celebrates the opening of its new exhibition Treasures of the Silk Road on Friday, September 25th, 4:00 pm-6:00 pm EDT.
The exhibit features over 70 musical instruments from the Pastel-Daneshgar musical instrument collection, with a focus on strings, flutes, and percussion from across Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Crafted from wood, snakeskin, horsehair, lambskin, camel bone, and other unique materials, these instruments provide a compelling history of cultural and artistic exchanges that have led to the myriad musical sounds and styles that permeate the world today. The opening event will feature remarks from the collection owner, Shahyar Daneshgar, and will feature musical clips provided by the Lotus World Music & Arts Festival.
Shahyar Daneshgar is a lifelong musician, scholar, and cultural ambassador whose passion for traditional music has shaped more than three decades of collecting, teaching, and performing. Born into a large musical family, he studied at the Tehran Conservatory of Music before pursuing academic work in Germany and later at Indiana University, where he earned his Ph.D. in Central Eurasian Studies in 1995. He taught at Indiana University until his retirement in 2024. He is founder and director of the Bloomington Silk Road Ensemble.
The exhibition is free and runs from September 25, 2026, to September 2027.
The mission of the McCalla Center is to provide accessible exhibition and educational experiences, creating opportunities for students, faculty, and the community to engage with collections, IU-generated creative activity, and community projects in meaningful and innovative ways.

description: Vindication Swim tells the remarkable story of Mercedes Gleitze, who in 1927 became the first British woman to swim the English Channel. Facing press hostility, anti-immigrant bias, and constraints on women in sport, Mercedes' achievement remains a powerful testament to her grit, courage, and determination. Writer-director Elliott Hasler—only 23 when the film premiered—pursued period authenticity through grassroots collaboration with coastal communities throughout the UK. Three years in the making, the film's swimming sequences were shot miles out in the Channel, vividly capturing the perils of Mercedes' epic crossing. [98 min; drama; English]A Q&A with director Elliott Hasler and Radhika Parameswaran (Herman B Wells Endowed Professor, Media School) will follow the screening.  Co-sponsored by the IU School of Public Health–Bloomington and The Media School.

title: Jazz @ the BCT: Natalie Boeyink Jazz Ensemble
description: About the DirectorNatalie Boeyink, bassist and educator, serves as associate professor of music jazz studies at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. After earning her doctorate in music education at the Jacobs School in 2015, Boeyink spent eight years as a jazz lecturer and senior lecturer in the University of North Carolina system. She earned an M.M. in Jazz Performance at the University of Louisville and a B.M. in Jazz Studies at Jacobs. Her interest in the educational experiences and careers of jazzwomen has launched a series of research projects, conference presentations and publications, including her dissertation, "An Analysis and Description of Female Jazz Instrumentalists." An advocate for jazzwomen, Boeyink served as chair of the Jazz Education Network's Women in Jazz Committee and worked to reestablish the Sisters in Jazz Collegiate Combo Competition. Batuquê Trio is Boeyink's seasoned collaboration with drummer Andy Smith and pianist Jamaal Baptiste. Focusing on contemporary Brazilian, Afro-Cuban, and Caribbean jazz, the trio frequently appears at jazz festivals as performers and clinicians. Their first CD, Transparency, was released in 2015. A second album is forthcoming in 2024. Some of Boeyink's notable performances include appearances with Tammy McCann, Jamie Baum, Ingrid Jensen, Terri Lyne Carrington, Christine Jensen, Leni Stern, Jovino Santos Neto, Joe Piscopo, David "Fathead" Newman, Jon Hendricks, Jeff Coffin, David Liebman, and Lorraine Feather.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: In Search of Freedom: Stories of Afghanistan Exhibition
description: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan  OPEN SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 - DECEMBER 4, 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM  OPEN 5-8 PM ON FIRST FRIDAYS OF THE MONTHIn Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistancelebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural,August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan.Organized in partnership with Indiana University's Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.The exhibition brings together Qahar's vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan's history, traditions, and everyday beauty - withAugust 15: A Mural for Afghanistan,a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. Developed through art therapy workshops with Afghan artists Zainab Ahmadi and Fawzia Abdaly, the mural preserves the participants' voices, memories, hopes, and resilience. The mural stands as a record of collective experience and a tribute to those who continue to seek safety, dignity, and freedom against all odds.Together, the artworks present a deeply human portrait of displacement, resilience, and belonging, inviting visitors to reflect on the the universal connections that unite us across borders, traditions, and generations, and the enduring human desire for freedom.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Samuel Levi Jones: An Archaeology of Knowledge
location: Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University, 1133 E. 7th Street, Fine Arts Plaza, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
For more than a decade, Indiana-born Samuel Levi Jones has created abstract assemblages with found printed and bound matter, deconstructing encyclopedias, law books, medical texts, and other didactic materials. Jones removes their fabric covers and pulps their pages, sewing these swatches together and applying paper pulp to create texturally rich, collaged works with raw edges, loose threads, and worn surfaces. His process of physically destroying archival materials and reconstructing them into artworks constitutes a materially engaged critique of institutional authority, reflecting on systems of knowledge that uphold power and privilege in the United States. For his exhibition at the Eskenazi Museum, Jones mined the museum’s collection for works that resonate with the themes he interrogates, including nationalism and patriotism, censorship, and the representation marginalized identities in historical narratives. Borrowing its title from the ideas of the influential French philosopher Michel Foucault, Samuel Levi Jones: An Archaeology of Knowledge comprises ten years of Jones’ investigations into the underlying structures that shape how we see, speak, and think about culture, politics, and power.
Support for this exhibition has been generously provided by the Robert and Sara LeBien Director's Endowment, Charlie and Jeanetta Nelms, and Janice L. Wiggins.

title: The Photographic Reflex: The Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. Collection
location: Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University, 1133 E. 7th Street, Fine Arts Plaza, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
Spanning more than 150 years, The Photographic Reflex celebrates a transformative gift to the Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University: more than one hundred works by eighty artists, generously donated by Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. This exhibition features photographs dating from 1856 to 2017 and highlights the medium’s extraordinary range, both as a tool for documentation and as a vehicle for artistic exploration.
From Alfred Stieglitz’s delicate studies of grass to Richard Misrach’s vast images of the cosmos, photographers have long found inspiration in the natural world. The built environment has also served as a compelling subject, and the exhibition includes Berenice Abbott’s striking views of 1920s New York City as well as Edward Burtynsky’s sweeping industrial landscapes.
Photography has played a central role in witnessing conflict, from Timothy H. O’Sullivan’s Civil War battlefield to iconic images from World War II, Vietnam, and beyond. While often associated with straightforward depictions of reality, photography also allows artists to experiment with light, exposure, and process to construct imaginative scenes and images beyond human sight.
The Photographic Reflex: The Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. Collection reveals photography’s power to reflect and shape our perception of the world around us across time, space, and vision.
Lead support for this exhibition has been generously provided by the Martha and David Moore Prints, Drawings and Photographs Endowment; Peter and Pamela DePrez; Anne Marks Morgan; Gregory Morse; Efroymson Family Fund; Anne N. DePrez; John J. Medveckis; and Friends of Lee Marks and John DePrez Jr.
Additional support provided by John M. (Jack) Reynolds, Jeffrey A. Wolin, Sandi Clark, and Katherine Campbell and Robert J. Boeglin Jr., M.D.

description: Outfitting IU Athletics: Hoosier Champions                  This exhibit showcases objects from IU's championship teams and athletes, connecting them to historic achievements in the Big Ten and the national stage. Dates: November 14, 2025 - October 2026                                      By Their Own Hands: The Black Filmmakers Hall of Fame!          Founded in 1974 by the Culture and Ethnic Affairs Guild of the Oakland Museum of California, the Black Filmmakers Hall of Fame began as a film lecture series and awards ceremony celebrating achievements of Black film industry figures. When that organization closed, they donated their materials to IU. In collaboration with the IU Black Film Center and Archive, this exhibit features objects from that collection, including founding documents, costumes, and handprints of inductees to the Hall of Fame.        Dates: September 2025 - December 2026                                      Capturing the Campus: T.C. Steele, Indiana University's First Artist in ResidenceCapturing the Campus pays tribute to renowned Hoosier artist T.C. Steele. The exhibit honors the century that has passed since his death by showcasing paintings form the artist's residency at IU and other relevant works. The exhibit will bring together Steele's landscapes from the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection and the Indiana State Museum and Historic Sites' collection, allowing the holdings of these two collections to be viewed in one space.        Dates: April 17, 2026 - April 2026                   Multipurpose Room          Currently Featuring: The Gift of Collecting: Tina Jernigan          Jernigan was a passionate supporter of both Indiana University and the arts. She donated artworks to the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection upon her passing in 2024. With funding provided by Jernigan, Public Art professionally framed, hung, and preserved these pieces for this exhibit in the McCalla Building and for future installations on campus.         Dates: July 2026-July 2027

title: Global Health Research Speaker Series - Dr. Alka Khaitan
description: Join the IU Center for Global Health and the Regenstrief Institute's Center for Health Services Research for this quarter's Global Health Research Speaker Series session featuring Alka Khaitan, MD (https://medicine.iu.edu/faculty/43672/khaitan-alka)  Professor of Clinical Pediatrics, Indiana University School of Medicine and Ryan White Center for Pediatric Infectious Diseases and Global Health"Beyond Viral Suppression: Immune Dysregulation and HIV Persistence in Perinatal HIV"  Antiretroviral therapy has transformed perinatal HIV into a chronic, treatable condition, yet viral suppression does not fully restore immune health or eliminate persistent HIV reservoirs. This talk will explore the long-term immunologic consequences of perinatal HIV and how immune dysregulation may intersect with HIV persistence. Research from a Kenyan cohort of children with perinatal HIV will provide insight into how the immunologic effects of HIV acquired early in life may persist despite treatment and relate to long-term health outcomes and barriers to HIV cure.  Dr. Khaitan is a professor of clinical pediatrics in the Division of Pediatric Infectious Diseases at Indiana University School of Medicine and the Ryan White Center for Pediatric Infectious Diseases and Global Health. Her research focuses on the long-term immunologic consequences of perinatal HIV, including chronic inflammation, immune activation and exhaustion and viral persistence. She leads NIH-funded research in the United States and Kenya examining how the timing and effectiveness of antiretroviral therapy shape immune health and long-term outcomes in children with HIV. She is also involved in pediatric HIV cure research through the IMPAACT Network and serves on the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Pediatric Antiretroviral Guidelines Panel.  This session is being held both virtually (via Teams webinar) and in-person. If you plan to attend the session in-person at the Regenstrief Institute you must register by Thursday, November 5th at 10 am Eastern Time and indicate this choice when you register.    Additionally, please take note of the following in-person details:In-Person Location: Regenstrief Institute (Room 209/210), 1101 W. 10th Street, Indianapolis (corner of 10th Street and Wilson Street)  Parking: Public (for fee) parking is available in the Wilson Street Garage which is adjacent to the building.  Building Security: Regenstrief maintains a secure building entrance. Event support from the Center for Global Health and the Center for Health Services Research will be onsite to assist with entry and other event logistics.

title: In Front of the Work: An Archeology of Knowledge
location: SIDNEY AND LOIS ESKENAZI MUSEUM OF ART
description: Rhonda and Anthony Moravec Gallery, Center for Prints, Drawings, and Photographs, Third Floor  This hour-long gallery conversation brings together perspectives from contemporary artandthelaw. GuestsreflectonJones'spowerfulworkandexplorequestionsofhistory,systemsofknowledge,power,andrepresentation.  Featured guests:I. India Thusi is a Professor of Law and Charles L. Whistler Faculty Fellow at the Indiana University Maurer School of Law and a Senior Scientist at the Kinsey Institute. Her scholarship examines how law constructs, regulates, and polices race, sexuality, vice, and gender. She is the author of Policing Bodies: Law, Sex Work, and Desire in Johannesburg (Stanford University Press), an ethnographic and legal study of sex work policing in South Africa. Her articles have appeared in the Harvard Law Review, New York University Law Review, California Law Review, Northwestern University Law Review, Georgetown Law Journal, UCLA Law Review, and other leading journals. Elliot Josephine Leila Reichert is an American curator, critic, and editor. She is the inaugural Curator of Contemporary Art at the Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University and was a 2023-24 Propel Fellow with the Association of Art Museum Curators Foundation. Reichert has curated critically acclaimed exhibitions and published widely in leading art journals.

title: Treasures of the Silk Road
location: McCalla Center, McCalla Center, 525 E. 9th Street, Bloomington, IN 47408
description:
The McCalla Center, in collaboration with musician and scholar Shahyar Daneshgar, celebrates the opening of its new exhibition Treasures of the Silk Road on Friday, September 25th, 4:00 pm-6:00 pm EDT.
The exhibit features over 70 musical instruments from the Pastel-Daneshgar musical instrument collection, with a focus on strings, flutes, and percussion from across Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Crafted from wood, snakeskin, horsehair, lambskin, camel bone, and other unique materials, these instruments provide a compelling history of cultural and artistic exchanges that have led to the myriad musical sounds and styles that permeate the world today. The opening event will feature remarks from the collection owner, Shahyar Daneshgar, and will feature musical clips provided by the Lotus World Music & Arts Festival.
Shahyar Daneshgar is a lifelong musician, scholar, and cultural ambassador whose passion for traditional music has shaped more than three decades of collecting, teaching, and performing. Born into a large musical family, he studied at the Tehran Conservatory of Music before pursuing academic work in Germany and later at Indiana University, where he earned his Ph.D. in Central Eurasian Studies in 1995. He taught at Indiana University until his retirement in 2024. He is founder and director of the Bloomington Silk Road Ensemble.
The exhibition is free and runs from September 25, 2026, to September 2027.
The mission of the McCalla Center is to provide accessible exhibition and educational experiences, creating opportunities for students, faculty, and the community to engage with collections, IU-generated creative activity, and community projects in meaningful and innovative ways.

title: Matthew Mindrup: Architecture Forgets, An Alternative View | Lecture
description: Buildings and cities, Mindrup argues, endure not by remaining unchanged but by repeatedly relinquishing what they once were.  Mindrup is an architect, scholar, and associate professor of architecture at the University of Sydney, where he directed the multidisciplinary Bachelor of Architecture and Environments from 2019 to 2025. He is a senior fellow of the Higher Education Academy and has taught architecture at institutions in the United States, Switzerland, Canada, and Australia.  His forthcoming book, "Architecture Forgets: The Art and Tactics of Transformation" (MIT Press, 2026), turns from how architecture comes into being to how it changes over time.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: In Search of Freedom: Stories of Afghanistan Exhibition
description: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan  OPEN SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 - DECEMBER 4, 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM  OPEN 5-8 PM ON FIRST FRIDAYS OF THE MONTHIn Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistancelebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural,August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan.Organized in partnership with Indiana University's Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.The exhibition brings together Qahar's vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan's history, traditions, and everyday beauty - withAugust 15: A Mural for Afghanistan,a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. Developed through art therapy workshops with Afghan artists Zainab Ahmadi and Fawzia Abdaly, the mural preserves the participants' voices, memories, hopes, and resilience. The mural stands as a record of collective experience and a tribute to those who continue to seek safety, dignity, and freedom against all odds.Together, the artworks present a deeply human portrait of displacement, resilience, and belonging, inviting visitors to reflect on the the universal connections that unite us across borders, traditions, and generations, and the enduring human desire for freedom.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.

title: Samuel Levi Jones: An Archaeology of Knowledge
location: Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University, 1133 E. 7th Street, Fine Arts Plaza, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
For more than a decade, Indiana-born Samuel Levi Jones has created abstract assemblages with found printed and bound matter, deconstructing encyclopedias, law books, medical texts, and other didactic materials. Jones removes their fabric covers and pulps their pages, sewing these swatches together and applying paper pulp to create texturally rich, collaged works with raw edges, loose threads, and worn surfaces. His process of physically destroying archival materials and reconstructing them into artworks constitutes a materially engaged critique of institutional authority, reflecting on systems of knowledge that uphold power and privilege in the United States. For his exhibition at the Eskenazi Museum, Jones mined the museum’s collection for works that resonate with the themes he interrogates, including nationalism and patriotism, censorship, and the representation marginalized identities in historical narratives. Borrowing its title from the ideas of the influential French philosopher Michel Foucault, Samuel Levi Jones: An Archaeology of Knowledge comprises ten years of Jones’ investigations into the underlying structures that shape how we see, speak, and think about culture, politics, and power.
Support for this exhibition has been generously provided by the Robert and Sara LeBien Director's Endowment, Charlie and Jeanetta Nelms, and Janice L. Wiggins.

title: The Photographic Reflex: The Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. Collection
location: Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University, 1133 E. 7th Street, Fine Arts Plaza, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
Spanning more than 150 years, The Photographic Reflex celebrates a transformative gift to the Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University: more than one hundred works by eighty artists, generously donated by Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. This exhibition features photographs dating from 1856 to 2017 and highlights the medium’s extraordinary range, both as a tool for documentation and as a vehicle for artistic exploration.
From Alfred Stieglitz’s delicate studies of grass to Richard Misrach’s vast images of the cosmos, photographers have long found inspiration in the natural world. The built environment has also served as a compelling subject, and the exhibition includes Berenice Abbott’s striking views of 1920s New York City as well as Edward Burtynsky’s sweeping industrial landscapes.
Photography has played a central role in witnessing conflict, from Timothy H. O’Sullivan’s Civil War battlefield to iconic images from World War II, Vietnam, and beyond. While often associated with straightforward depictions of reality, photography also allows artists to experiment with light, exposure, and process to construct imaginative scenes and images beyond human sight.
The Photographic Reflex: The Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. Collection reveals photography’s power to reflect and shape our perception of the world around us across time, space, and vision.
Lead support for this exhibition has been generously provided by the Martha and David Moore Prints, Drawings and Photographs Endowment; Peter and Pamela DePrez; Anne Marks Morgan; Gregory Morse; Efroymson Family Fund; Anne N. DePrez; John J. Medveckis; and Friends of Lee Marks and John DePrez Jr.
Additional support provided by John M. (Jack) Reynolds, Jeffrey A. Wolin, Sandi Clark, and Katherine Campbell and Robert J. Boeglin Jr., M.D.

description: Outfitting IU Athletics: Hoosier Champions                  This exhibit showcases objects from IU's championship teams and athletes, connecting them to historic achievements in the Big Ten and the national stage. The items featured in the exhibit are from the IU Athletics Sports Memorabilia Collection and feature photos and videos provided by IU Athletics and Indiana University Archives.                Dates: November 14, 2025 - October 2026                                      By Their Own Hands: The Black Filmmakers Hall of Fame!          Founded in 1974 by the Culture and Ethnic Affairs Guild of the Oakland Museum of California, the Black Filmmakers Hall of Fame began as a film lecture series and awards ceremony celebrating achievements of Black film industry figures. When that organization closed, they donated their materials to IU. In collaboration with the IU Black Film Center and Archive, this exhibit features objects from that collection, including founding documents, costumes, and handprints of inductees to the Hall of Fame. Steele, Indiana University's First Artist in ResidenceCapturing the Campus pays tribute to renowned Hoosier artist T.C. Steele. The exhibit honors the century that has passed since his death by showcasing paintings form the artist's residency at IU and other relevant works. The exhibit will bring together Steele's landscapes from the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection and the Indiana State Museum and Historic Sites' collection, allowing the holdings of these two collections to be viewed in one space.
